planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto thin, well-drained soil beneath an open canopy so winter cold-stratifies it naturally; established plants resent heavy, wet ground and are slow to bulk up from seed, so many restorationists use nursery plugs instead.

directions: Rough-leaved ricegrass is an early, cool-season bunchgrass of thin, rocky dolomite- and sandstone-derived soils in Driftless Area oak savanna and goat prairie, where its evergreen basal leaves persist through winter and its inconspicuous flower spikes appear before most other prairie grasses have even greened up. Unlike nearly every other native prairie grass, it tolerates and even favors dappled shade beneath an open bur oak or white oak canopy, making it a useful textural groundcover on dry, lean woodland edges where typical sun-loving bunchgrasses fail. Its broad, rough-margined basal leaves distinguish it at a glance from the narrow-leaved ricegrasses (some current grass treatments place this species in the genus Piptatherum instead), and seed should be collected and sown fresh since it loses viability quickly in storage.

planting.note: Set out container or bare-root stock in spring into cool, well-drained, often rocky or gravelly soil in dappled shade; it establishes readily on talus and ravine slopes where cold air drainage keeps roots cool through summer.

directions: Round-leaved dogwood is a boreal shrub that reaches its southern outliers on the cool, north-facing talus and dolomite ravine slopes of the Driftless Area, where cold air venting and mossy rock keep its roots shaded and moist through summer heat. Its nearly circular, opposite leaves and purple-blotched young twigs distinguish it readily from the narrower-leaved dogwoods that share these ravines, and flat clusters of white spring flowers give way to pale blue-white drupes relished by grouse and songbirds. In cultivation it wants the same cool, humus-rich, well-drained footing as its wild sites and spreads slowly by root suckers into a loose multi-stemmed thicket rather than a single trunk.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare, thin sand or gravel rather than transplanting, since the thick taproot resents disturbance; a dormant fall sowing also works and lets winter cold break any seed dormancy.

directions: Prairie fameflower is a diminutive, taprooted succulent that roots directly in bare sand and thin soil over exposed dolomite and sandstone bedrock on Driftless Area bluff prairies and sand barrens, sites too dry and mineral-poor for most tallgrass competitors. Its fleshy, cylindrical leaves store water for the drought of a bedrock outcrop, and its small pink flowers open for only a few hours in the heat of a sunny afternoon before closing again, a trait that gives the genus its common name. Because the taproot is brittle and slow to reestablish, it is best started from seed sown directly where it will grow rather than transplanted, and it needs sharp drainage and full sun to persist from year to year.

planting.note: Dormant-seed in fall so the long awns and seed cold-stratify over winter; full sun and lean, well-drained soil over bedrock or gravel reproduce its native goat-prairie footing best.

directions: Porcupine grass is a cool-season bunchgrass of thin, bedrock-controlled dolomite and sandstone prairies, the steep south-facing 'goat prairies' that dot the unglaciated Driftless Area where soil is too shallow over rock for the tallgrass sod of glacial-till prairie to form. Each seed trails a long, sharply bent, twisting awn that drills the grain into the ground (or into grazing animals) as it dries and untwists, a mechanical seed-dispersal trick unique among the region's native grasses. It flowers and sets seed earlier than most warm-season prairie grasses, giving goat prairies a distinctive silvery, awned look by early summer, and it persists best in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall onto saturated, mineral-rich ground for natural winter stratification, or set out spring plugs; it needs permanently wet, cold groundwater-fed soil and will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Buxbaum's sedge is a blue-green, tufted sedge of cold, spring-fed fens and sedge meadows, the same calcareous groundwater seeps that feed the algific talus slopes of the Driftless Area and keep their soil chilled year-round. Its glaucous foliage and dark, almost black-scaled spikes set it apart from the many paler fen sedges it often grows beside, and it tolerates the mineral-rich, calcium-charged water typical of dolomite bedrock drainage. In a garden setting it demands a permanently saturated, alkaline bog or spring-fed swale rather than ordinary moist soil, and once correctly sited it spreads gradually by short rhizomes with no need for fertilizing or division.

planting.note: Fall-sow onto lean, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in sun to light shade; this rhizomatous sedge spreads to knit together loose, dry ground and needs no supplemental moisture once established.

directions: Dry-spike sedge colonizes the driest ground in the Driftless Area plant community, from thin soil over exposed dolomite and sandstone outcrops to sand prairie and open oak savanna, spreading by slender rhizomes into loose, drought-tolerant colonies. Its wiry, narrow leaves and small, pale, short-awned spikes give it a wispy, understated look that blends into bedrock-controlled bluff prairie rather than drawing attention, and it is exceptionally drought tolerant once its rhizomes establish. It is a useful soil-stabilizing groundcover for lean, well-drained garden sites that most moisture-loving sedges cannot tolerate, asking only sun to light shade and sharp drainage.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall into lean, well-drained sandy or rocky soil beneath an open canopy; it forms low, loose tufts and is slow to bulk up, so many restoration plantings use nursery-grown plugs.

directions: Rough-seeded sedge, sometimes called parachute sedge for its oddly inflated, papery seed capsules, grows in old fields, exposed rock outcrops, and open oak woods on the shallow, well-drained soils typical of Driftless Area savanna and bedrock-controlled prairie. It fruits earlier than most woodland sedges, often finishing seed by early summer, and its low, loose tufts tolerate both dry shade and more open, sun-exposed rocky ground where competing vegetation is sparse. It asks only lean, sharply drained soil and is useful for restoring texture and early-season structure to dry savanna and glade plantings.
